nameStory: The "mermaidweed" name comes from this aquatic plant's delicate, feathery underwater leaves that sway gracefully like a mermaid's hair in the current. The "comblike" part refers to how these submerged leaves are divided into fine, parallel segments that resemble the teeth of a comb. Early botanists thought these ethereal underwater fronds looked magical enough to belong in fairy tales!
description: Comblike mermaidweed is a small aquatic plant that lives both underwater and at water's edge, growing 6-20 inches tall. It's a shape-shifter that looks completely different depending on whether its leaves are submerged or growing above water. Underwater, it has delicate, feathery leaves, while above water it develops simple, tooth-edged leaves. This humble wetland plant produces tiny, inconspicuous flowers and often forms small colonies in shallow water.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The key identifying feature: underwater leaves are deeply divided into fine, hair-like segments (like a feather or comb), while leaves above water are simple with toothed edges. Feel the submerged leaves - they're soft and collapse when lifted from water.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers with no petals bloom in summer, tucked in the angles where leaves meet the stem. You'll need to look closely - they're easily missed and feel like small bumps along the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a low, somewhat sprawling plant that can be completely submerged, floating at the surface, or rooted in wet soil at water's edge. Stems feel smooth and slightly succulent.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, hard, three-sided nuts that feel rough to the touch and often persist into fall. Each tiny fruit has three distinct ridges you can feel with your fingertip.

habitat: Look for comblike mermaidweed in shallow ponds, slow streams, ditches, and wetland edges throughout New England, though it's quite uncommon. It prefers acidic, nutrient-poor waters and muddy or sandy bottoms. You'll often find it growing alongside other aquatic plants like water lilies, pondweeds, and sedges in quiet backwaters.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges underwater as delicate, feathery leaves unfurl. This is when the plant is most visible and the leaf differences are most dramatic.
seasonality.summer: Tiny flowers bloom from June through August, and you can see both underwater feathery leaves and above-water simple leaves on the same plant.
seasonality.fall: Small three-sided fruits ripen and the plant begins to die back. Above-water leaves may turn yellowish before withering.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely, persisting only as seeds in the mud and potentially some underwater root structures in milder areas.

funFact: This plant is like an aquatic Jekyll and Hyde - it can completely change its leaf shape depending on whether it's underwater or in air, with some plants showing both leaf types at once when water levels fluctuate!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with water milfoils, which also have feathery underwater leaves, but water milfoils have leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem, while mermaidweed leaves alternate up the stem. Memory trick: "Mermaidweed alternates like a mermaid swimming side to side."
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's related to seaweeds, mermaidweed is actually a flowering plant in the water milfoil family, not a true aquatic "weed" or marine plant. The "Proserpinaca" genus name comes from Proserpina, the Roman goddess who moved between worlds - fitting for a plant that lives both above and below water!
compareHints: The only other mermaidweed in New England is marsh mermaidweed, which typically grows in wetter soils rather than open water and has less dramatically feathered underwater leaves. Marsh mermaidweed's submerged leaves are more coarsely divided, while comblike mermaidweed's are finely divided into thread-like segments. When in doubt, look at the habitat - comblike prefers open water, marsh prefers muddy shores.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The only other mermaidweed in our region is combleaf mermaidweed, which has more consistently comb-like (pectinate) leaves and is less common in New England.
